briefing:
The Istanbul Summit working groups will determine whether NATO survives success. Russia's offer is on the table: status quo transit restoration, mutual nuclear de-escalation, cyber cease-fire, in exchange for NATO Ukraine/Georgia expansion moratorium and energy sanctions relief. The terms are substantive but not sovereignty-compromising. Lithuania's 89% war support can potentially accept this - it's not territorial concession but political concession (Ukraine/Georgia). The question is whether NATO consensus holds on those terms.

The Article 7 success removed Hungarian obstruction but created new tension - Orbán will challenge the suspension through CJEU and has begun coordinating with Slovakia and Serbia on 'Central European sovereignty' messaging. If the Istanbul deal succeeds and vindicates diplomacy over military response, Orbán's 'I told you so' narrative gains strength domestically despite losing his veto.

Germany's stabilization at 20% war support is fragile - Bundestag budget passage bought time but didn't reverse decline. If Istanbul negotiations extend beyond 48 hours, German opinion may resume collapse. Trump at 15% faces similar constraints - Congressional Republicans gave him two weeks maximum. The clock is ticking.

Working groups negotiate four tracks: (1) Military de-escalation sequencing, (2) Nuclear posture verification, (3) Ukraine/Georgia moratorium language, (4) Sanctions relief scope. Details will determine success or collapse.
narrative:
The twelve hours before the Istanbul Summit became a crucible for European unity. At 06:00 CET, the European Council voted 23-4 on Article 7 suspension of Hungarian voting rights. France's energy diplomacy with Greece and Austria, combined with UK and Dutch pressure, secured the four-fifths majority. Only Hungary, Slovakia, Austria, and Cyprus voted against. Viktor Orbán's veto power was suspended for the duration of the crisis - a constitutional earthquake in EU governance. Hungary's transit blockade remained, but its ability to obstruct NATO decisions during the summit vanished.

The Article 7 success reshaped the Istanbul dynamics. President Trump's acceptance of the expanded format (US-RU-LT-PL-TR-NATO-EU from the outset) eliminated Russia's bilateral strategy. When delegations arrived in Istanbul at 11:00 CET, Poland and Lithuania sat as equals with Washington and Moscow. Chancellor Merz's Bundestag address at 10:00 CET stabilized German opinion - the emergency defense budget passed 386-302, halting the collapse at 20% war support. Germany's commitment firmed just as the summit convened.

Russia's strategic calculus shifted. NATO's unity exceeded Moscow's expectations - UK carrier deployment, French nuclear submarine, Nordic hardline, and Trump's refusal to pressure Lithuania created a unified front Putin could not split. The 72-hour cyber suspension was extended another 24 hours as a 'good faith gesture,' signaling Russian willingness to de-escalate. The opening Istanbul session revealed Russia's genuine offer: return to status quo transit in exchange for NATO nuclear de-escalation to peacetime, no Ukraine/Georgia expansion commitment, and energy sanctions relief. No permanent corridor demand remained.

The Lithuanian delegation, backed by unanimous European support, accepted negotiations on these terms while maintaining absolute red lines: no corridor 'feasibility studies,' no compromise on sovereignty, and Seimas ratification required. The summit structure - opening plenary, working groups, final session - prevented procedural traps. As delegations broke for working groups at 12:00 CET, the crisis had transformed from military confrontation to genuine diplomatic negotiation. Whether it would succeed remained uncertain, but alliance fracture had been averted.
